title: Programming Language Forge
tagline: Languages as instruments, not identities — Python, Java, C++, and the systems beneath them.
blurb: IL-03 forges the programming backbone: Python, Java, and C++ taught as instruments with shared ideas (OOP, generics, streams, concurrency) compared across languages; data structures and algorithms as the single canonical node for the whole university; systems software from computer organization to software engineering; the MIT 6-3 course sequence as a reference layer; and a generative-art studio where code becomes visual craft. Original katas, bug zoos, race-condition laboratories, and cross-language exercises throughout — with Noah as Socratic debugging coach.

modules.title: The Programming Backbone: Python, Java, C++, DSA
modules.summary: Welcome to IL-03: Programming Language Forge. I'm your instructor, and over four modules we're going to forge the programming backbone every serious engineer stands on — languages as instruments, data structures and algorithms as the canonical craft, and debugging as a discipline. This is Module 1: The Programming Backbone — Python, Java, C++, and DSA. We take the three languages in sequence because each teaches what it's best at: Python for fluency and the standard library, Java for OOP discipline and the type system, C++ for the memory model and zero-cost abstraction. DSA grows alongside — every structure you implement in the language of the week, analyzed from first principles. And throughout it all, Noah is your Socratic debugging coach: hypothesis first, hints second.
objectives: Write idiomatic code in Python, Java, and C++, translating ideas across all three.
Implement arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs; analyze sorting, divide-and-conquer, and dynamic programming.
Apply SOLID, the working set of design patterns, and refactoring with before/after discipline.
Write correct concurrent code: threads, virtual threads, async/await, locks — and reproduce races before fixing them.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **instrument, not identity** — Python, Java, and C++ are tools with strengths; the lesson is choosing the right one for the job, not pledging allegiance to one.
- **generator** — A Python iterator produced lazily with `yield`; items are computed on demand with O(1) memory, so pipelines can handle inputs that never fit in RAM.
- **context manager** — The `with`-block protocol (`__enter__`/`__exit__`); guarantees cleanup — files closed, locks released — even when exceptions fly.
- **duck typing** — Python's protocol-oriented OOP: if it quacks (`__len__`, `__iter__`), treat it as a duck. Dunder methods are the protocols; ABCs (abstract base classes) are the explicit interfaces.
- **PECS** — Producer Extends, Consumer Super: `? extends T` when reading from a generic (producer), `? super T` when writing into it (consumer). If you can't explain PECS, you don't know Java generics yet.
- **lazy stream** — Java's intermediate stream ops (filter, map, peek) do nothing until a terminal op (collect, forEach) runs; they fuse and execute per element.
- **virtual thread** — Java 21's lightweight thread: thread-per-task at massive scale for I/O-bound work. Caveat: `synchronized` blocks pin carriers — prefer `ReentrantLock`.
- **RAII** — Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: constructors acquire, destructors release; smart pointers (`unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`) make ownership explicit, so leaks are impossible by construction.
- **rule of five** — If you define any of destructor, copy/move constructor, copy/move assignment, define (or delete) all five. (Or follow the rule of zero: let the compiler do it.)
- **move semantics** — `std::move` plus rvalue references eliminate copies; the transfer of ownership instead of duplication is the core of modern C++ performance.
- **undefined behavior (UB)** — Code the standard doesn't define: use-after-free, data races, signed overflow, uninitialized reads. The compiler owes you nothing afterwards — learn to predict UB from reading code.
- **Big-O** — A comparative tool, not a prophecy: n log n vs n² at n=10⁶ is the difference between a second and a lifetime. Always ask best/average/worst, and the space-time trade-off.
- **dynamic programming** — Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems: memoize first, tabulate second. Recognize the pattern before reaching for it.
- **race condition** — Two threads interleaving read-modify-write (`counter += 1` is three bytecodes: LOAD, ADD, STORE) so updates get lost. Reproduce the race first — a fix for a bug you can't reproduce is a guess.
- **SOLID** — Five design principles for maintainable OOP; the D (Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions) is the seam that makes testing possible.
- **canonical node** — This module's DSA material is the single canonical algorithms node for the whole university; IL-08 deepens the theory, nothing is duplicated.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
The forge runs on a weekly rhythm: one language, one structure, one race, one pattern. Python week: every script lab from scratch, and you write a failing test *first* — the bug zoo below assumes test-first discipline. Java week: PECS drills until reflexive, then trace one stream pipeline by hand each day, annotating each op LAZY or TERMINAL. C++ week: UB drills — predict the nasal demons before the compiler shows them to you.

1. **Generator pipeline lab** — Build the data pipeline two ways: list-based and generator-based, and measure peak memory with `tracemalloc` on a large input (see scriptLab il03-lab-generators). The required fragments force the laziness comparison.
2. **PECS exercise** — Write a method taking `List<? extends Number>` (producer: read-only) and one taking `List<? super Integer>` (consumer: safe to add Integer). Get the bounds backwards once on purpose, read the compiler error, fix it.
3. **Race laboratory** — Write the threaded counter from scriptLab il03-lab-race, run it, and observe the shortfall (expected 400000, got less). Only then fix it with a `Lock`. Show the bug BEFORE the fix.
4. **BST degeneration** — Implement the binary search tree in scriptLab il03-lab-bst: insert [5,3,7,1,9], verify inorder is sorted (the invariant). Then insert range(1000) sorted and measure the height — 1000, a linked list. That's why AVL and red-black exist.
5. **Build toolchain** — Compile a two-translation-unit C++ program by hand: compile each to an object file, then link. Watch a header-guard mistake produce a link error, and learn what the linker is telling you.
6. **Before/after refactoring** — Take one of your own week-one scripts and refactor it against a SOLID checklist (single responsibility first). Keep both versions; the diff is the lesson.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your deliverable is a **cross-language kata portfolio**: one problem, solved in all three languages, with analysis. Pick any three of the following — (a) a seeded word-frequency counter over a large text file, (b) an LRU cache with O(1) get/put, (c) Dijkstra over a generated graph, (d) a thread-safe bounded queue, (e) a JSON pretty-printer.

For each kata you ship four artifacts: the Python solution (idiomatic: comprehensions, generators, context managers), the Java solution (typed: PECS-correct generics, a stream pipeline where it fits), the C++ solution (memory-honest: RAII, no raw `new`/`delete`, move where it pays), and a one-page analysis — Big-O of time and space, where each language helped or hurt, and which solution you'd ship and why. Include the test suite you wrote first and a bug-zoo entry: one bug you hit, the hypothesis you stated to Noah before the fix, and the fix.

This is the university's canonical DSA node, so the bar is the implementation being *yours*: every structure hand-written once, every analysis done from first principles. Noah grades the reasoning, not just the green tests.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah is your Socratic debugging coach for this module — hypothesis first, hints second. Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- Show Noah your threaded counter shortfall. What's your hypothesis for *where* the interleaving happens — which of the three bytecodes? Don't reach for the lock until you can narrate the race.
- Trace this stream pipeline by hand, annotating each operation LAZY or TERMINAL, and tell Noah exactly when `filter` first executes: `list.stream().filter(...).map(...).collect(toList())`.
- Read this C++ snippet and predict: is it UB, and which kind? `int a[2]; a[2] = 5;` — then argue *why* the compiler is allowed to do anything at all.
- Explain PECS to Noah as if Noah were a junior: why is `List<? super Integer>` safe to *add* Integer to, but not safe to *read* Integer from?
- *Bug zoo ritual:* before any fix, state your hypothesis out loud. If the hypothesis is wrong, the zoo gets an entry — wrong hypotheses are the tuition you pay for right ones.

cards.back: Laziness — they produce items on demand with O(1) memory, enabling infinite/large sequences and pipelined processing.
Producer Extends, Consumer Super: ? extends T when reading, ? super T when writing.

cards.front: Java streams: when does a filter execute?
cards.back: Only when a terminal operation runs — intermediate ops are lazy and fused per element.
Resource lifetime bound to object lifetime: constructor acquires, destructor releases — no leaks by construction.
If you define any of destructor, copy/move constructor, copy/move assignment — define (or delete) all five.
Non-negative edge weights. Negative weights need Bellman-Ford.
Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems → memoize first, tabulate second.
First reproduce the race in the sandbox, then fix it — a fix for a bug you can't reproduce is a guess.

quiz.q: What does this print? xs = [1,2,3]; it = (x*2 for x in xs); xs.append(4); print(list(it))
quiz.explain: Generators are lazy — the expression evaluates when consumed, seeing the appended 4 (see the generator entry in the Concepts section).

quiz.q: Java: List<? super Integer> l — what can you add?
quiz.explain: Consumer super: safe to add Integer; the list holds Integer or a supertype (PECS, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: C++: which is undefined behavior?
quiz.explain: Out-of-bounds write — classic undefined behavior; the compiler owes you nothing afterwards (see UB in the Concepts section).

quiz.q: Best worst-case guarantee among quicksort/mergesort/heapsort?
quiz.explain: Heapsort is O(n log n) worst-case in-place; quicksort degrades to O(n²) without randomization (Big-O, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: BFS on an unweighted graph gives ___.
quiz.explain: BFS explores in increasing distance — first visit is via the fewest edges (covered in the Project brief's Dijkstra kata).

quiz.q: SOLID's 'D' (DIP) says ___.
quiz.explain: Dependency Inversion: high-level modules depend on abstractions — the seam that makes testing possible (SOLID, from the Concepts section).

modules.title: Systems Software: Organization to Software Engineering
modules.summary: Welcome back to the Forge. I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Systems Software — from computer organization to software engineering. Module 1 gave you instruments; this module gives you the substrate every program runs on: how bits become data, how the OS juggles processes, how packets cross the network, how databases keep their promises, and how software gets built by teams. Concepts here become commands in IL-04's Linux path and designs in IL-08's theory track — learn the idea here, type it there. We close with the full-stack capstone: scoped, built, deployed, and presented against a public rubric — the artifact IL-10's career path will present as evidence.
objectives: Explain data representation, the memory hierarchy, and caching performance effects.
Describe processes, scheduling, memory management, and filesystems as an OS designer would.
Write sockets code; debug networks with packet-level tools.
Design relational schemas, write complex SQL, and reason about transactions and indexes.
Ship a full-stack capstone: scoped, built, deployed, presented.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **two's complement** — The signed-integer representation where addition 'just works' and there is a single zero; the reason your CPU doesn't need separate add/subtract circuits.
- **fetch-decode-execute** — The CPU's heartbeat: fetch the instruction, decode it, execute it — on registers, billions of times per second.
- **memory hierarchy** — Registers → L1/L2/L3 cache → RAM → SSD: each level bigger and slower. Performance lives or dies here, not in the ALU.
- **locality** — Temporal (reuse the same data soon) and spatial (use nearby data soon). Caches exploit both; the row-major vs column-major matrix exercise makes a ~10x difference you can measure.
- **process vs thread** — A process owns an isolated address space; a thread shares its process's address space. Shared memory is the power and the peril.
- **virtual memory** — The OS's great illusion: every process gets its own address space, and the MMU plus page tables maintain it. A page fault means the MMU found no mapping — the OS pages it in, or kills the process.
- **starvation** — What happens when a scheduler (FCFS, round-robin, priorities) never gets around to a waiting task; priorities without aging are the classic cause.
- **inode** — The filesystem's metadata record: permissions, ownership, block pointers — everything about a file except its name.
- **OSI model** — Seven layers used as a troubleshooting map: when the app fails, work bottom-up (physical → link → network → transport → ...) and find the first broken layer.
- **TCP vs UDP** — TCP: reliability plus ordering at a latency cost. UDP: speed with app-managed reliability. Chat wants ordering (TCP); games and voice often take UDP with custom recovery.
- **ACID** — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the transaction contract a database makes with you.
- **3NF** — Third normal form: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key — the rule that eliminates transitive dependencies.
- **index trade-off** — Indexes speed WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY on their columns (B-trees underneath) and cost on every write. Design is trade-off; EXPLAIN is the truth serum.
- **test pyramid** — Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, fewest slow end-to-end tests at the top. Invert it and your suite becomes a boat anchor.
- **REST contract** — Resources modeled as URLs, verbs with semantics (PUT is idempotent — repeating it converges; POST typically creates anew), versioned and documented so a client you didn't write can conform to it.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This module is a laboratory arc: measure first, then believe. The cache exercise, the sockets series, and the query gym all follow the same ritual — predict, measure, explain.

1. **Cache locality measurement** — Write the matrix traversal twice (row-major and column-major) over a large matrix and time both. The ~10x gap is spatial locality made physical; write down which layout C uses and why it wins.
2. **Sockets project series** — Build the TCP echo server (blocking), then add `select`, then a threaded version, then the chat server. Feel the C10k problem in your own code before learning its solutions.
3. **Packet-level debugging** — With the chat server running, debug a deliberately broken client using ping, traceroute, dig, curl, and a packet capture. Read the capture: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — the handshake, in the wild.
4. **Schema design** — Model a small domain (orders, customers, products) to 3NF on paper, then deliberately denormalize one table for read performance and document *why* — denormalize deliberately, never by accident.
5. **Query gym** — Against a real database, write the graded queries (joins, aggregation, subqueries), run EXPLAIN on each, and add the composite index that kills the full table scan. Record the before/after plans — the decision record is the deliverable, not just the fast query.
6. **Contract-first API** — Write the API contract first (resources, verbs, auth shape: sessions vs tokens vs OAuth), then implement to it. Your API is graded by a client you didn't write — conformance tests are the specification.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your deliverable is the **full-stack capstone**, staged like a real engagement: scoping, implementation, deployment, presentation.

**Scope ruthlessly.** One page: the problem, the user, the three features that matter, and the five you're cutting. The cut list is graded — restraint is the skill.

**Build it end to end.** Frontend (HTML/CSS, JavaScript: DOM, events, fetch), backend API (contract-first: REST resource modeling, auth, versioning, documentation), relational database (3NF schema, indexes justified with EXPLAIN output). The test pyramid governs: unit-heavy, integration in the middle, a thin e2e cap.

**Deploy and present.** Ship it somewhere real, then present against the public rubric: does it run, is the schema sane, is the API contract honored, is the scope honest? This artifact travels with you — IL-10's career path presents it as portfolio evidence, so the README must explain the system to a stranger in five minutes.

Agile practice runs underneath the whole build: a backlog with hygiene, standups with yourself (or your team), and a retro at each stage gate. The SDLC model you pick — waterfall, agile, spiral — must be justified in the scope document: when each fits is part of what you're proving you know.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- Explain your cache-exercise numbers to Noah: why did row-major win, which cache level did the win come from, and what would change the result?
- Your chat server uses TCP. Argue the UDP case to Noah anyway — what would you have to build yourself to make UDP chat acceptable, and when would it be worth it?
- Show Noah your EXPLAIN before and after the composite index. What did the planner do differently, and what does the index cost you on every INSERT?
- Walk Noah through one scheduling scenario: round-robin with a CPU-hog and an interactive task — who starves, and what fixes it?
- Defend your capstone cut list: which five features died, and what would have broken if you'd kept them?

cards.back: One representation for signed integers where addition 'just works' and there's a single zero.
Temporal: reuse the same data soon. Spatial: use nearby data soon. Caches exploit both.
Process: isolated address space. Thread: shared address space within a process — shared memory is the power and the peril.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the transaction contract.
Every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration, fewest slow e2e at the top.

quiz.q: Row-major vs column-major traversal on a large matrix: the lesson?
choices: cache locality — one can be ~10x faster
quiz.explain: Spatial locality: row-major matches C's layout — the cache-line effect is measurable and huge (see locality in the Concepts section, measured in the Hands-on procedure).

quiz.q: A page fault means ___.
choices: the MMU found no mapping — the OS must resolve it
quiz.explain: Page fault = address not currently mapped; the OS pages it in (or kills the process if invalid) — virtual memory, from the Concepts section.

quiz.q: TCP vs UDP for a chat server: the real trade-off?
choices: TCP: reliability+ordering at latency cost; UDP: speed with app-managed reliability
quiz.explain: Choose by requirements: chat wants ordering (TCP); games/voice often take UDP + custom recovery (TCP vs UDP, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
quiz.explain: 3NF: non-key attributes depend only on the key — no transitive chains (see 3NF in the Concepts section).

quiz.q: An index on (last_name) speeds up ___.
choices: WHERE last_name = ? and ORDER BY last_name
quiz.explain: Indexes serve lookups/sorts on their columns; they cost on writes and don't help unindexed scans (index trade-off, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: Contract-first API exercise: who grades your API?
quiz.explain: Conformance tests from an independent client — the contract is the specification (from the Hands-on procedure's contract-first exercise).

modules.title: MIT 6-3 Reference Layer
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3: the MIT 6-3 Reference Layer. I'm your instructor, and this module is a map, not a territory. MIT's Electrical Engineering & Computer Science curriculum — 6.100A/B Python, 6.1200 discrete math, 6.1210/6.1220 algorithms, 6.1910 computation structures, 6.1800/6.1810 systems, 6.3900 machine learning — distilled into prerequisite order as a study layer over MIT OpenCourseWare's public materials. The platform's rules govern this layer: no duplicated courses (overlap routes to the single canonical node), prerequisite gates before the algorithms and ML nodes, and honest pacing adapted for solo learners. Use it as a reading and problem-set guide; the deep study lives in the IL modules it points to.
objectives: Sequence the 6-3 curriculum in prerequisite order with a personal study schedule.
Use the 6.100A/B problem sets as the Python practice spine.
Bridge 6.1200's discrete math into IL-02's canonical discrete node — no duplicated courses.
Gate the algorithms and ML nodes on verified prerequisites.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **6.100A/B** — Introduction to Computer Science Programming in Python. Its problem sets are the practice spine of this layer: done in order, with Noah for Socratic help when stuck.
- **6.1200** — Mathematics for Computer Science: proofs and induction, number theory for CS, graph theory, probability for computing. The discrete-math bridge into IL-02's canonical discrete node.
- **induction template** — Base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step — until it's muscle memory. This is the proof technique the algorithms courses assume you already own.
- **number theory for CS** — Modular arithmetic, gcd, Fermat's little theorem: the RSA prerequisites, and the reason 6.1200 matters to security engineers.
- **6.1210 / 6.1220** — Introduction to / Design and Analysis of Algorithms: sorting, hashing, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming — gated on discrete-math fluency, because algorithm analysis is applied discrete math.
- **6.1910** — Computation Structures: the climb from digital logic to the processor, assembly and the machine, caches and virtual memory — the hardware/software interface.
- **6.1800 / 6.1810** — Computer Systems Engineering / Operating System Engineering: design principles at scale, taught through the classic design papers.
- **end-to-end argument** — A 6.1800 design-paper staple: place function at the endpoints of the system unless there's a compelling reason not to. Read every design paper asking what problem, what insight, what trade-off.
- **6.3900** — Introduction to Machine Learning: the on-ramp map, not the territory. The platform runs a prerequisite audit (IL-02 linear algebra + probability) before opening it; the territory is IL-07 and IL-16.
- **canonical-node rule** — The global rule: where OCW overlaps an IL module (6.1200 vs IL-02's discrete module, 6.1210 vs Module 1's DSA), the platform routes to the single canonical node. No duplicated courses, ever.
- **term-structure honesty** — OCW problem sets assume MIT's term structure: recitations, office hours, a cohort. Solo learners get adapted pacing — one problem set per week per course is a full-time pace.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This layer is walked, not watched. The procedure turns six course catalogs into one personal curriculum.

1. **Build the sequence** — Lay out the six courses in prerequisite order (6.100A/B → 6.1200 → 6.1210/1220 → 6.1910 → 6.1800/1810 → 6.3900) and mark every canonical-node overlap: wherever OCW duplicates an IL module, write down the IL node you'll use instead.
2. **Set the cadence** — One problem set per week per course is full-time pace. Be honest about your hours and pick one course at a time; the schedule is a contract with yourself.
3. **Run the prerequisite audit** — Before opening 6.1210: can you do an induction proof cold? Before 6.3900: have IL-02's linear-algebra and probability nodes verified? Gates are there to save you from opaque proofs, not to slow you down.
4. **Work the 6.100A/B problem sets** — In order, with Noah: hypothesis first, hints second. The problem sets are the Python practice spine of Module 1's language work.
5. **Simulator labs for 6.1910** — Build the ALU in the digital-logic simulator *before* reading about pipelining. The gates-first arc only works if your hands go first.
6. **Active paper reading** — For each 6.1800/6.1810 design paper, write one paragraph: the problem, the insight, the trade-off. A paper you can't summarize in a paragraph is a paper you haven't read.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your deliverable is a **personal 6-3 study plan**: a document that could hand to a stranger and have them walk the layer.

It contains: the six courses in your chosen order with the canonical-node substitutions marked (which IL modules replace which OCW overlaps, and why); your weekly cadence with the honesty math (hours available, problem sets per week, finish dates); the prerequisite gates you'll clear and how you'll verify each one; and a reading list of five 6.1800/6.1810 design papers with your one-paragraph problem/insight/trade-off summaries for two of them as samples.

The plan is graded on honesty, not ambition: a sustainable twelve-month plan beats a heroic three-month plan that dies in week four. Include the failure protocol — what you do when you fall two problem sets behind (answer: re-pace, don't cram; the term-structure honesty note applies to your plan too). Revisit the plan monthly; a study plan is a living document or it's fiction.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- State your study order for the six courses and justify each prerequisite edge — why can't 6.1210 come before 6.1200?
- Do an induction proof cold for Noah (Noah picks the claim). The template should be muscle memory by now.
- Show Noah your canonical-node substitution map: where does OCW overlap IL-02 and Module 1's DSA, and which node wins each overlap?
- Summarize one design paper in a single paragraph — problem, insight, trade-off — then defend why the trade-off was the right call.
- What's your failure protocol? Walk Noah through exactly what happens to the plan when life costs you two weeks.

cards.back: 6.100A/B Python → 6.1200 discrete math → 6.1210/1220 algorithms → 6.1910 computation structures → 6.1800/1810 systems → 6.3900 ML.

cards.front: Global rule when OCW overlaps IL-02?
cards.back: No duplicated courses — route to the single canonical node (IL-02's discrete module).
Prerequisite audit: IL-02 linear algebra + probability nodes verified first.
Base case → inductive hypothesis → inductive step. Muscle memory.
One paragraph per paper: the problem, the insight, the trade-off.

quiz.q: Why does the platform gate 6.1210 on discrete math?
choices: algorithms proofs need induction and asymptotics fluency
quiz.explain: Algorithm analysis is applied discrete math — without induction and Big-O fluency, the proofs are opaque (see the prerequisite-audit step in the Hands-on procedure).

quiz.q: 6.1910's arc in four steps?
quiz.explain: Computation Structures climbs from gates to the hardware/software interface (6.1910, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: The honest note about OCW problem sets?
choices: they assume MIT's term structure — pacing is adapted for solo learners
quiz.explain: Recitations and office hours don't exist for solo learners — the study guide re-paces accordingly (term-structure honesty, from the Concepts section).

quiz.q: Where does deep ML study live?

modules.title: Generative Art: Circle Packing
modules.summary: Welcome to the studio — Module 4: Generative Art: Circle Packing. I'm your instructor, and this is where precision becomes aesthetics. We build a circle packer from first principles: rejection sampling with a seeded RNG, then Poisson-disc sampling, then front-chain packing, all accelerated by spatial grids. Then parameters become a design language — Span, Factor, NC, Alpha, AngleX/AngleY, blend modes — each value a deliberate decision. And because we work from inspiration, we close with the ethics: attribution, inspired-by vs copied, and the lab notebook as experimental method. Three studies, one packer, your voice.
objectives: Implement an honest rejection-sampling circle packer with a seeded RNG.
Upgrade to Poisson-disc and front-chain packing with spatial grids.
Read and write parameter blocks as design decisions.
Keep a lab notebook; attribute inspiration honestly; produce three studies.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **rejection sampling** — Propose a random candidate circle; reject it if it collides; repeat. Honest, simple, and slow enough to *feel* the algorithm.
- **seeded RNG** — The same seed produces the same piece. Reproducibility is the difference between art and accident — and between a debuggable program and a mystery.
- **Poisson-disc sampling** — Minimum-distance guarantees between samples via the grid-accelerated dart-throwing algorithm: even coverage without clumping.
- **front-chain packing** — Grow from the boundary inward, placing each new circle tangent to the existing front. Denser, more deliberate compositions than pure rejection.
- **spatial grid** — Uniform-grid hashing that makes collision checks O(1) amortized: the difference between a sketch and a system.
- **Span** — The spacing parameter: breathing room vs density. Read it as the piece's lung capacity.
- **Factor** — The size-falloff parameter: visual hierarchy, large to small.
- **NC** — Hue layers: palette depth, how many color voices the piece speaks in.
- **Alpha** — Opacity: the atmosphere and layering depth of the piece.
- **AngleX / AngleY** — Field tilt: implied light or gravity, the direction the composition leans.
- **blend mode** — Compositing math (multiply, screen, overlay): how layers converse. Know what the pixels do, not just what looks good.
- **seeded variation** — Controlled surprise: the seed varies, the design language stays. Same instrument, different performance.
- **lab notebook** — Seed, parameters, intent, result, next experiment — every study gets an entry. Experimental method applied to aesthetics.
- **inspired-by vs copied** — Same idea plus your parameters plus your notebook = inspired. Same parameters with no transformation = copied. Lineage is a feature; name it.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build the packer in layers, and watch the composition quality jump at each one. Keep the lab notebook open from step one — every study gets an entry.

1. **Rejection sampler** — Implement the honest version: seeded RNG, propose a random (x, y, r), reject on collision with any placed circle, repeat until N placed or attempts exhausted. Render it. It will be slow and sparse — that's the baseline.
2. **Spatial grid** — Add uniform-grid hashing for collision checks (O(1) amortized). Measure the speedup at N=2000; the grid is what turns the sketch into a system.
3. **Poisson-disc upgrade** — Replace pure rejection with grid-accelerated dart throwing enforcing a minimum distance. Compare the coverage: no more clumping, no more voids.
4. **Front-chain packing** — Implement boundary-inward growth, each circle tangent to the front. Compare density against Poisson-disc on the same seed.
5. **Parameter block** — Expose Span, Factor, NC, Alpha, AngleX/AngleY, and blend mode as one block. Read it like a score: each value is a choice about the piece's physics.
6. **One-parameter experiments** — Change exactly one parameter at a time; record the effect in the notebook (seed, parameters, intent, result, next experiment). Ten experiments minimum before the three studies.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your deliverable is **three studies from one packer**: same instrument, three distinct parameter voices — breadth proves the instrument, not the accident.

Study 1 — *Density*: push Span low and Factor steep; document where the composition breaks (overlap artifacts, muddy blends) and where it sings. Study 2 — *Atmosphere*: Alpha low, blend modes doing the work; the piece should feel like weather. Study 3 — *Tilt*: AngleX/AngleY carrying the composition; implied light or gravity must read at a glance.

Each study ships with its lab-notebook entry (seed, parameters, intent, result, next experiment) and an attribution line: name what inspired it — the Pattlas piece, a parameter block you read, a paper on sampling — explicitly. Inspired-by means your parameters plus your notebook plus your transformation; the lineage section of each entry states what you took and what you changed. Honest attribution is graded alongside the pixels: a beautiful study with a missing lineage fails the ethics bar.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- Show Noah your rejection sampler's collision check. Where's the O(n²) hiding, and exactly how does the spatial grid kill it?
- Read your own parameter block back to Noah like a score: defend each value as a design decision. Which one would you change first, and what would you expect?
- Compare your Poisson-disc and front-chain renders on the same seed: which is denser, which is more even, and which would you choose for a poster vs a texture?
- State the inspired-by vs copied test for your Study 2: what did you take, what did you transform, and where's the lineage recorded?
- Your notebook's 'next experiment' column: pick the most interesting one and argue why it's the right next move.

cards.back: Propose random candidates; reject on collision; repeat. Honest, simple, slow.
Same seed → same piece. Reproducibility separates art from accident.
Minimum distance between samples — even coverage, no clumping.
O(1) amortized collision checks via uniform-grid hashing.
Span = spacing (density). Factor = size falloff (hierarchy).
Same idea + your parameters + notebook = inspired. Same parameters, no transformation = copied.

scriptLabs.title: Lazy Pipeline: Generators vs Lists
scriptLabs.brief: Build a data pipeline two ways — list-based and generator-based — and measure peak memory on a large input. The required fragments force the laziness comparison.
scriptLabs.hint: Generator version: sum(x*x for x in range(n) if x % 2). tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[1] is peak.

scriptLabs.title: Race Laboratory: Produce It, Then Fix It
scriptLabs.brief: Write a threaded counter increment that loses updates (the race), demonstrate the loss, then fix it with a lock. You must show the bug BEFORE the fix — a fix for an unreproduced bug is a guess.
scriptLabs.starter:
import threading

counter = 0

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        counter += 1  # race here

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print('expected 400000, got', counter)
# 1) run: observe the shortfall  2) fix with a lock  3) re-run: exact
scriptLabs.hint: Wrap the increment: lock = threading.Lock(); with lock: counter += 1. The with-block is the critical section.
scriptLabs.solution:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:          # critical section: read-modify-write is atomic now
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print('expected 400000, got', counter)  # now exactly 400000
# Lesson: counter += 1 is three bytecodes (LOAD, ADD, STORE) — threads interleave between them.

scriptLabs.title: BST: Implement, Then Break, Then Balance-Talk
scriptLabs.brief: Implement a binary search tree with insert and inorder traversal. Then insert sorted data and observe the degeneration — the lab's point is feeling why balanced trees exist.
scriptLabs.hint: Height of degenerate sorted-insert tree = n-1. Inorder of a BST is always sorted — that's the invariant to test.

scenarios.title: Choosing the Language for the Job
scenarios.context: You need: a CLI tool parsing 10GB of logs fast, and a web dashboard for the results. One language or two?

options.text: C++ or Rust-class systems language — throughput is the requirement
options.why: 10GB parsing is throughput-bound; zero-cost abstraction and memory control win. Python would work but 10-50x slower.
Write-speed doesn't matter if runtime misses the SLA — and the dashboard needs the data on time.

options.text: Python (Flask/FastAPI) or JS — ecosystem speed for CRUD + charts
options.why: Dashboards are I/O-bound glue — the ecosystem (ORMs, chart libs, auth) matters more than raw speed.
Possible, miserable: you'd hand-roll what web frameworks give for free. Instruments, not identities.

scenarios.title: The Slow Query
scenarios.context: A dashboard query on orders (10M rows) takes 14s. EXPLAIN shows a full table scan on WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ?.

options.text: Add a composite index on (customer_id, status)
options.why: The query filters on both columns — a composite index serves the WHERE directly. Verify with EXPLAIN after.

options.text: Add more RAM to the database server
options.why: Hardware masks the problem at 10M rows and bankrupts you at 100M. Fix the access path first.

options.text: Cache the whole table in Redis
options.why: Caching helps repeated identical queries but the scan still happens on miss — and invalidation becomes your new problem.

steps.prompt: After the index, it's 40ms. What do you document?

options.text: The index definition, the before/after EXPLAIN, and the write-cost trade-off
options.why: Indexes cost on every write — the decision record lets the next engineer reason about it.
Undocumented performance fixes get reverted by the next migration. The lab notebook habit applies to production too.

mockTasks.prompt: SQL: customers with no orders over $100 (keep all customers).

FROM customers c
-- complete the join
mockTasks.answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 100 WHERE o.id IS NULL;
mockTasks.explain: Filter in ON preserves the outer join; WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps only customers with no big orders.

Python: refcount + GC · Java: GC, escape analysis · C++: RAII, unique/shared_ptr, no GC — you own it
Binary search O(log n) · Quicksort avg O(n log n), worst O(n²) · Mergesort O(n log n) · Heapsort O(n log n) in-place · BFS/DFS O(V+E) · Dijkstra O(E log V) (non-negative weights)
Hash table avg O(1) · BST avg O(log n), worst O(n) · Heap: min/max O(1), insert/extract O(log n) · Trie: prefix O(k)
Filter nullable side in ON not WHERE · UNION removes dupes, UNION ALL keeps · Index the WHERE/JOIN columns · EXPLAIN before optimizing
Process ≠ thread · Page fault = unmapped address · TCP: reliable+ordered · UDP: fast, app-managed reliability · OSI: troubleshoot bottom-up

answerBank.q: Which language should I learn first?
answerBank.a: Python — fastest to fluency, gentlest error messages, largest library. Then Java for type discipline, then C++ for the memory model. The order is pedagogical, not tribal.

answerBank.q: How do I actually get good at DSA?
answerBank.a: Implement every structure once by hand, analyze every algorithm's complexity, then do timed problems. The implementation is the understanding; the analysis is the interview skill. IL-08 deepens the theory later.

answerBank.q: Java streams confuse me — where do I start?
answerBank.a: Internalize laziness first: intermediate ops (filter/map/peek) do nothing until a terminal op (collect/forEach) runs. Trace the IL-09 stream lab by hand, annotating LAZY vs TERMINAL per line.

If you touch systems, games, embedded, high-frequency, or browsers — yes. Otherwise, learn enough to read it: RAII, pointers vs references, and why UB is the exam's favorite trap. The memory honesty transfers everywhere.

answerBank.q: How do MIT OCW courses fit a solo learner?
answerBank.a: Use the 6-3 sequence as a reading/study guide with the adapted pacing in Module 3 — one problem set per week per course is full-time pace. Verify prerequisites (discrete math before algorithms) via the gates.

It's algorithms with aesthetic output: sampling theory, spatial data structures, experimental method. The studio trains precision (parameters as decisions) and documentation (lab notebooks) — both production skills.
